mentions.quote: slavery never exists for a Brahmin
Even a man of the same caste should never make a Brahmin a slave. For by the slavery of a Brahmin, the king's majesty is diminished.
never a Brahmin, says Bṛhaspati
a best of the twice-born should not perform any impure task
even a Brahmin is to be killed
He who takes a Brahmin woman or sells her, the king should annul that act

entities.description: The priestly/scholarly caste exempt from enslavement and impure labor, whose degradation is said to diminish royal authority.
entities.justification: Brahmins are consistently named as a category bearing special legal immunity from slavery across chapters 63 and 67.

mentions.quote: Slavery is in the natural order of the castes, not in the reverse order, for a Kshatriya, Vaishya, and Shudra who renounce their independence.
mentions.role: caste subject to slavery in natural order

mentions.quote: A Kshatriya, Vaishya, or Shudra may sometimes be made to perform the work of a slave by one of the same caste
mentions.role: caste that may be enslaved within caste

mentions.quote: the king should banish a Brahmin, and make a Kshatriya or Vaishya a slave

entities.description: The warrior caste, which unlike Brahmins can be enslaved within natural caste order or punished by the king with enslavement.
entities.justification: Kshatriyas are explicitly named alongside Vaishyas and Shudras as castes subject to slavery in chapter 63.

mentions.quote: Slavery is in the natural order of the castes, not in the reverse order, for a Kshatriya, Vaishya, and Shudra who renounce their independence.
the king should banish a Brahmin, and make a Kshatriya or Vaishya a slave

entities.description: The merchant/farming caste, which may be enslaved within natural caste order as punishment for abandoning ascetic vows.
entities.justification: Vaishyas are named in chapter 63 among castes subject to slavery in natural caste ordering.

mentions.quote: But a Shudra he may make a slave, whether bought or not. For he was created by the Self-existent One for servitude itself.
mentions.role: lowest caste, inherently subject to servitude

mentions.quote: for a Kshatriya, Vaishya, and Shudra who renounce their independence

entities.description: The servile caste declared by Katyayana to have been created for servitude, and therefore enslaved freely by the king.
entities.justification: The Shudra is singled out in chapter 63 (p-18a088) as uniquely created for slavery by the Self-existent One.

mentions.quote: Bhṛgu declares that slavery arises from the voluntary surrender of one's independence, like that of a wife.
For cutting off the ear, lip, nose, foot, eye, tongue, penis, or hand, the highest fine; for splitting them, the middle fine, says Bhṛgu.
mentions.role: cited legal authority on bodily injury

mentions.quote: Household utensils, vehicles, milch animals, ornaments, and servants, being visible, are divided. Bhṛgu said the treasury is divided when it is concealed.
What is acquired by a promise of learning, and what is received from a pupil … this is wealth acquired through learning, says Bhṛgu.
Whatever law of a country, caste, corporation, or village has been declared by Bhṛgu, one should arrange the partition of inheritance according to that.
Property that was mutually concealed … should be divided in equal shares, says Bhṛgu.
A pasture for cows … is for use and not to be divided … says Bṛhaspati.
mentions.role: cited authority (note: this verse credits Bṛhaspati, not Bhṛgu)

mentions.quote: What is received by a woman out of affection after her marriage ceremony from her husband or parents, that is a subsequent gift (*anvādheya*), says Bhṛgu.

entities.description: A revered Vedic sage cited repeatedly throughout these chapters as a primary authority on slavery, inheritance partition, bodily injury fines, and women's property.
entities.justification: Bhṛgu is invoked by name as a law-giving sage in chapters 63, 66, 71, 72, 73, and 75 to authorize specific legal rulings.

mentions.quote: never a Brahmin, says Bṛhaspati
whatever wealth is acquired through valor is to be divided, says Bṛhaspati
Bṛhaspati says one should know that as wealth acquired through learning (*vidyādhana*), not to be divided
A pasture for cows, its protection, and clothing worn on the body are for use and not to be divided … says Bṛhaspati.

entities.description: A sage-lawgiver cited as an authority on slavery restrictions for Brahmins, on wealth acquired through valor, and on categories of impartible property.
entities.justification: Bṛhaspati is quoted by name in chapters 63 and 72 as a legal opinion holder whose rulings the text endorses.

mentions.quote: For causing the death of living beings, one should give a substitute for it, or one should give its equivalent value; thus said Manu.
mentions.role: cited legal authority on compensation for killing

mentions.quote: The followers of Manu say that thieves caught with the stolen goods should be banished immediately.
mentions.role: cited school of legal opinion on theft

entities.description: The primordial lawgiver whose pronouncements on compensation for killing animals and on punishment of thieves are cited as authoritative precedents.
entities.justification: Manu is named as a direct authority in chapter 66 (p-8d2588) and his school is mentioned in chapter 68 (p-1ecf0c).

mentions.quote: This is disliked by the followers of Gautama, as it is censured for destroying a living being.
mentions.role: dissenting legal school on punishment of thieves

entities.description: A legal authority whose school disputes the Manu school's ruling that thieves caught with goods should be immediately banished, on grounds of ahiṃsā.
entities.justification: The followers of Gautama are contrasted with Manu's followers in chapter 68 (p-1ecf0c) on the question of punishing thieves.

mentions.quote: Guarded in iron fetters, on a meager diet, and being strong, they should perform work for the king until death; thus says Kauśika.
mentions.role: cited legal authority on penal labor for thieves

entities.description: A lawgiver who prescribes lifelong penal servitude in iron fetters for thieves as an alternative to banishment or mutilation.
entities.justification: Kauśika is named as the source of the ruling on lifetime forced labor for thieves in chapter 68 (p-ecceef).

mentions.quote: The virtuous woman who, after her husband's death, remains established in celibacy, she, with conduct like Arundhatī's, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
mentions.role: exemplar of wifely chastity and celibacy

entities.description: The celestial exemplar of wifely virtue and celibacy after widowhood, invoked as the ideal model for a widow who remains chaste.
entities.justification: Arundhatī is named in chapter 70 (p-198921) as the paradigmatic virtuous widow, whose world is the world of Brahmā.

mentions.quote: she, with conduct like Arundhatī's, is glorified in the world of Brahmā
mentions.role: divine realm promised to virtuous widows

entities.description: The creator deity whose celestial world is promised as a posthumous reward for chaste widows who follow Arundhatī's example.
entities.justification: Brahmā's world (brahmaloka) is named in chapter 70 (p-198921) as the eschatological destination of the virtuous celibate widow.

mentions.quote: For he was created by the Self-existent One for servitude itself.
mentions.role: cosmic creator who ordained Shudra servitude

entities.description: The self-born creator deity (identified with Brahmā or Manu-Svāyambhuva) invoked to cosmologically justify the Shudra's servile status.
entities.justification: The Self-existent One is cited in chapter 63 (p-18a088) as the divine authority behind the social ordering that places Shudras in servitude.

mentions.quote: those contiguous to the contiguous neighbors are declared to be in the shape of a lotus
mentions.role: geometric metaphor for concentric neighborly witness rings

entities.description: Used as a spatial metaphor to describe the concentric arrangement of neighboring landowners whose testimony is relevant in boundary disputes.
entities.justification: The lotus-shape comparison in chapter 64 (p-0edb58) is a descriptive legal concept explaining the layered witness hierarchy.

themes.topic: Commercial law and rescission of sale

mentions.quote: Rescission of Sale and Purchase, and Non-Delivery after Sale
He who, having bought and received an article, does not take it, or does not give it if it is unflawed, shall, after paying a tenth part of the price, get his own article.
A fraudulent contract, an exchange, or an unequal transaction by more than a third, and a purchase made even by command, may be annulled within ten years.
Even with a small payment of the price, the validity of the sale is established.

themes.justification: Chapter 62 is entirely devoted to rules for rescinding commercial transactions, penalties for non-delivery, and criteria for valid versus void sales.

mentions.quote: Bhṛgu declares that slavery arises from the voluntary surrender of one's independence, like that of a wife.
But a Shudra he may make a slave, whether bought or not. For he was created by the Self-existent One for servitude itself.
He who has intercourse with his own female slave, and she gives birth from it … she should be made free, and she is not a slave along with her issue.

themes.justification: Chapter 63 systematically maps slavery onto caste order, defines its origins, specifies who may and may not be enslaved, and addresses the status of slave offspring.

themes.topic: Land rights, boundary determination, and neighborly testimony

mentions.quote: Boundary Disputes
Excess or deficiency in a share, its existence or non-existence, enjoyment without title, and the boundary—these are the six causes of a land dispute.
Sometimes, one person desired by both may trace the boundary, placing earth on his head, wearing red garments, and being composed.

In the ordeal of walking the boundary, in the ordeal of the sacred water, and in the ordeal of touching the foot, a divine or royal calamity is expected within three fortnights, a fortnight, or a week.

themes.justification: Chapter 64 is entirely organized around the causes, witnesses, and resolution procedures for boundary and land-title disputes, including divine ordeals.

themes.topic: Verbal injury, defamation, and its gradations

mentions.quote: Verbal Assault
A snort of contempt, a cough, and whatever is censured in the world, to imitate or repeat it, is called verbal assault (*vākpāruṣya*).
It is remembered as three-fold, due to its being harsh, abusive, or grave.

themes.justification: Chapter 65 classifies verbal injury into a three-tier taxonomy (harsh, abusive, grave) and specifies the conditions and fines for each type.

themes.topic: Physical violence, bodily injury, and proportionate punishment

mentions.quote: Physical Assault
When a blow is struck to cause pain to men or animals, the punishment should be inflicted in proportion to the pain caused.
In case of destruction of the body or a sense organ, just as the punishment is fixed, so also should compensation for satisfaction be given, and the cost of recovery (*samutthāna*).

themes.justification: Chapter 66 governs proportionate fines and compensation for bodily injury to both humans and animals, with specific attention to caste-sensitive scaling.

themes.topic: Violent crime (sāhasa), self-defense, and the felonious aggressor (ātatāyin)

mentions.quote: An act that is done with force (*sahasā*) is declared to be a violent crime (*sāhasa*).
One may kill without hesitation an aggressor who comes with the intent to destroy.
one who violates another's wife, and one who is intent on finding a weakness—one should know these and the like to be all felonious aggressors (*ātatāyins*).

themes.justification: Chapter 67 develops a specific legal concept of the ātatāyin (felonious aggressor) whose killing is lawful, and distinguishes categories of violent crime.

themes.topic: Theft, property seizure, and state responsibility for crime

mentions.quote: Theft
Whether secretly or openly, by night or by day, whatever seizure of another's property occurs, that is declared to be theft (*steya*).
Whatever is stolen from anyone in his own country must be restored by the king. The king should himself search for and recover what was lost.

themes.justification: Chapter 68 defines theft broadly and places royal responsibility for restitution at the center of the theft regime.

themes.topic: Sexual violence, complicity, and collective punishment

mentions.quote: When a man forcibly has carnal enjoyment with women, he should be put to death, for that is a transgression of duty.
The instigator, the accomplice, the one who shows the way, the one who gives shelter, the one who gives a weapon, and the one who gives food to wrongdoers
all are considered perpetrators of that act. One should fix a punishment for them according to their ability and role.

themes.justification: Chapter 69 extends criminal liability for sexual offenses to the full ring of enablers—instigators, helpers, bystanders—creating a doctrine of collective responsibility.

themes.topic: Wifely duty, chastity, and the ideal of the devoted wife

mentions.quote: A wife who is not separated from her husband, being disciplined, should serve the sacred fire, desiring good fortune, the state of non-widowhood, and being devoted to her husband.
The virtuous woman who, after her husband's death, remains established in celibacy, she, with conduct like Arundhatī's, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.

themes.justification: Chapter 70 articulates the normative ideal for a wife's behavior both during marriage (serving the sacred fire) and after the husband's death (celibacy).

themes.topic: Partition of inheritance: rules, shares, and eligibility

mentions.quote: Partition of Inheritance
When fathers and brothers take the entire mass of property in equal shares, that is called a righteous partition.
The son of a woman married out of order, one born from a person of the same *gotra*, and one who has abandoned his ascetic vows—they are not entitled to the inheritance.

themes.justification: Chapter 71 is an extensive treatment of inheritance shares, eligible heirs, and disqualifications, including distinctions based on caste and marriage order.

themes.topic: Impartible property: vidyādhana, valor-wealth, and strīdhana

mentions.quote: Impartible Properties
the wealth that is acquired by that learning is called wealth acquired through learning (*vidyāprāpta*).
Wealth acquired through valor and through learning, and what is remembered as Woman's Property (*strīdhana*)—all this is not to be divided by the heirs at a partition.

themes.justification: Chapter 72 systematically enumerates classes of property immune from partition at inheritance: skill-wealth, valor-wealth, and women's property.

themes.topic: Women's property (strīdhana): definition, types, and autonomy

mentions.quote: The Definition and Types of Woman's Property
Woman's Property (*strīdhana*) is remembered as six-fold.
Over *saudāyika* wealth, the independence of women is always declared, in sale and in gift at their pleasure, even in the case of immovable property.
Neither the husband, nor the son, nor the father, nor the brothers have power over *strīdhana* in taking or giving it away.

themes.justification: Chapters 75–76 constitute a dedicated treatise on strīdhana, establishing its six categories, its inviolability from male family members, and the one exception (saudāyika) where women have full independent disposal rights.

mentions.quote: In the ordeal of walking the boundary, in the ordeal of the sacred water, and in the ordeal of touching the foot, a divine or royal calamity is expected within three fortnights, a fortnight, or a week.
If one cannot determine the cause of a physical assault by motive and other means, one should employ witnesses or a divine ordeal there.

themes.justification: Divine ordeals appear across chapters 64 and 66 as a residual evidentiary device when documentary and testimonial proof fails, reflecting a shared theological-legal logic underlying the text.

themes.topic: King's duty to administer justice and protect subjects

mentions.quote: Whatever is stolen from anyone in his own country must be restored by the king. The king should himself search for and recover what was lost.
For by the slavery of a Brahmin, the king's majesty is diminished.
The king should carefully investigate what has been reported untruthfully.
Those who are destroyers of their own country and those who block the highways, the king, having confiscated all their property, should have them impaled on a stake.

themes.justification: Throughout chapters 65–68, royal duty appears as an implicit organizing principle: the king investigates, restores stolen property, protects Brahmins, and punishes banditry — this is a background norm enabling the entire legal framework.

themes.topic: Defect, fraud, and good faith in commercial transactions

mentions.quote: What was bought without being known to be defective, and is later found to be so, that must be returned to the owner if it is within the time limit.
He who, having shown a flawless article, delivers a flawed one, shall be made to pay double the price and an equal amount as a fine.
What is sold by one who is intoxicated or insane, or for a low price out of fear, or by one who is not independent or is deluded, that must be given back to him.

themes.justification: Chapter 62 implicitly constructs a doctrine of good-faith dealing: consent and accurate representation are treated as conditions of a valid sale, with fraud or incapacity voiding the transaction.

citations.quote: Bhṛgu declares that slavery arises from the voluntary surrender of one's independence, like that of a wife.
citations.justification: The text explicitly attributes this legal ruling to Bhṛgu, treating him as a named authoritative source within the dharmaśāstra tradition.

citations.quote: For cutting off the ear, lip, nose, foot, eye, tongue, penis, or hand, the highest fine; for splitting them, the middle fine, says Bhṛgu.
citations.justification: Bhṛgu is invoked as a named authority to confirm the graduated fines for bodily mutilation.

citations.quote: A Kshatriya, Vaishya, or Shudra may sometimes be made to perform the work of a slave by one of the same caste, but never a Brahmin, says Bṛhaspati.
citations.justification: Bṛhaspati is cited as the source of the rule restricting Brahmin enslavement.

citations.quote: For causing the death of living beings, one should give a substitute for it, or one should give its equivalent value; thus said Manu.
citations.justification: Manu is directly cited as the source of the rule on compensation for killing animals.

citations.quote: The followers of Manu say that thieves caught with the stolen goods should be banished immediately.
citations.justification: The Manu school is cited as one of two opposing positions on the punishment of thieves caught in the act.

citations.quote: This is disliked by the followers of Gautama, as it is censured for destroying a living being.
citations.justification: The Gautama school explicitly dissents from the Manu school position, making this a genuine intertextual dispute recorded in the text.

citations.quote: Guarded in iron fetters, on a meager diet, and being strong, they should perform work for the king until death; thus says Kauśika.
citations.justification: Kauśika is named as the authoritative source for the rule mandating lifetime penal labor for thieves.

citations.quote: Among brothers in a family who have been educated by their father, whatever wealth is acquired through valor is to be divided, says Bṛhaspati.
citations.justification: Bṛhaspati is the named source for the rule on dividing valor-wealth among educated brothers.

citations.quote: Bṛhaspati says one should know that as wealth acquired through learning (*vidyādhana*), not to be divided.
citations.justification: Bṛhaspati is cited to confirm that wager-won learning-wealth is impartible.

citations.quote: What is acquired by a promise of learning … this is wealth acquired through learning, says Bhṛgu.
citations.justification: Bhṛgu is named as the authority for this definition of vidyādhana.

citations.quote: A pasture for cows, its protection, and clothing worn on the body are for use and not to be divided … says Bṛhaspati.
citations.justification: Bṛhaspati is cited as the source of the rule on impartible use-property in chapter 72.

citations.quote: Whatever law of a country, caste, corporation, or village has been declared by Bhṛgu, one should arrange the partition of inheritance according to that.
citations.justification: Bhṛgu is invoked as a comprehensive legal authority whose rulings on local law govern inheritance partition.

citations.quote: Property that was mutually concealed … should be divided in equal shares, says Bhṛgu.
citations.justification: Bhṛgu is the named source for the rule on re-dividing discovered concealed property.

citations.quote: What is received by a woman out of affection after her marriage ceremony from her husband or parents, that is a subsequent gift (*anvādheya*), says Bhṛgu.
citations.justification: Bhṛgu is cited as the authority for classifying post-marriage gifts as anvādheya strīdhana.

citations.quote: Household utensils, vehicles, milch animals, ornaments, and servants, being visible, are divided. Bhṛgu said the treasury is divided when it is concealed.
citations.justification: Bhṛgu is cited to extend the partition rule to concealed treasury, contrasting with visible property.
